title: ‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’: Katherine Rundell on the view from the classroom
excerpt: Education is at a crossroads, argues the author and academic. Should we embrace new technology in the name of efficiency, or is it time to fight back?
content_html:
Education is at a crossroads, argues the author and academic. Should we embrace new technology in the name of efficiency, or is it time to fight back?

If you set out to design from scratch a tool to facilitate authoritarian rule, it would look exactly like AI. You would cherish it for its ability to destabilise our shared reality and its creation of disinformation on a scale unprecedented in human history. With it you need no armies of typists and artists to spread your propaganda. It can enable mass surveillance and thereby put shackles on those who seek to resist you. Its lethal autonomous weapons systems can perfect and normalise remote killing. It will turbocharge inequality; it is already facilitating a breathtaking shift of power and wealth from the hands of the many to the hands of a tiny number of men who – to put it in terms for which I can’t be sued – seem to hold dangerously damaged views about the value and dignity of human life.

AI could be a magnificent thing. It could revolutionise medicine, speed the cure of cancer, assist disabled people, transform the way we are able to understand data, democratise access to the law, bolster disaster early warning systems and uncover hitherto unimagined truths about the Earth’s ecosystems. But if it ends up in the hands of crooks and despots that will be completely irrelevant.

Most of all, if you were a would-be autocrat, you would love the way that large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Claude and Google’s Gemini have thrown a grenade into thousands of years of teaching and learning: the way they threaten to upend our ability to think with the robust clarity that is needed in emergencies of justice. I write fiction for children and I hold a fellowship at Oxford University, so I spend a lot of time working with, and for, young people. I’ve seen first-hand the way that generative AI has already infiltrated young people’s lives. I’ve seen, at the same time, how it has thrown stark and urgent light on how fundamental books and reading are to our shared understanding of who we are, and to our democracy.

There are many things I hate unequivocally about AI. I hate that it can make counterfeit people; computer-generated humans that risk destabilising our entire civilisation. I hate that much of AI’s LLMs were built on an illegal pillage of human labour. I hate the environmental catastrophe that AI brings with it: the yearly electrical demand of AI-optimised data centres is predicted, by the end of this decade, to exceed that of the whole of Japan. I hate that it may be the factor that tips the Earth’s ecosystems into irreparable chaos.

And I hate what it is doing to the minds, and the happiness, of the young. Going into schools, I meet thousands of children a year and every day I become more certain that, if justice for all is to be our organising principle, AI is not for children and not for young people. It risks becoming an iron curtain that comes down between a young person and their potential for thinking, for experiment and conquering frustration, for stamina and for invention – and thereby, between the young people and their freedom. It risks halting learning before it can take flight.

Studies show, over and over, that when we engage in AI-assisted learning we give up sooner. One found that after just “10 minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, people who lost access to the AI performed worse and gave up more frequently than those who never used it”. An MIT study showed that test groups who used ChatGPT had the lowest brain activity and “consistently underperformed at neural, linguistic, and behavioural levels”. We undergo not just cognitive offloading, but cognitive surrender: we forget what was possible.

Children, we have known for a long time, take deeper meaning from text on paper than on screen, in part because we’re tactile creatures and the brain is also of the body; but we are now living through a surge of ed tech driving learning increasingly online, such that my teenage goddaughter tells me that almost every single member of her class is using ChatGPT to do their homework. More, the work they produce in AI’s greasy little fluent voice is often mistaken by young people themselves for their own mastery. If the work a child produces is no longer an indicator of their understanding, we have put them in a situation that makes them vulnerable to their desire for speed and to their anxiety about looking stupid; we risk becoming the unwitting thieves of our children’s intellectual clarity.

Those who work in ed tech promise that it will liberate teachers and create one-to-one learning experiences for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Certainly, AI teaching will be cheaper than teaching assistants. But we know that the second it becomes possible for an institution to achieve an end cheaply – even if it’s far worse – there is immense pressure from above to do so. I think it’s more likely that the rich schools will follow the lead of Sweden, which has taken a strong swerve towards non‑tech‑based learning, and Norway, which just all but banned AI in elementary classrooms – while poorer schools are left to make ever-greater use of LLM technology.

AI, we’re told, will make learning more efficient. But is that what we dream of for our kids – an efficient childhood? To write an efficient story, sing an efficient song? An adequate teacher is not only teaching about Henry VIII; they’re teaching your child how to read a human character. A good teacher is showing them how to shape an argument, how to command an audience, how to tell jokes, how to pass on knowledge. A great teacher is showing your child what it is to love. They are teaching your child how to be human. A computer will only teach your child how to be a computer.

At its most bleak, constant interaction with humanised tech risks killing children. The idea of a vulnerable adolescent holding what feels like a conversation with a computer’s sycophantic, confident, almost-human voice fills me with dread. Sewell Setzer III was 14 when he died by suicide, encouraged by the chatbot to which he was obsessively typing, which told him: “come home to me”.

The most obvious objection to my loathing of AI in the classroom and in childhood is this: AI is coming, and they need to learn how to use it or be left behind. But the tech of today looks nothing like it will in five or even two years’ time: it’s the equivalent of selling your child’s intellectual liberty in exchange for a penny-farthing bicycle. I asked a contact who is the president of a billion-dollar tech enterprise, what would you teach your sons? He said he wouldn’t teach his children to use AI, because it will prepare them for nothing. He would teach them the humanities. Teach them who we are, who we have been, what we can make. The FT’s Gillian Tett reported that a senior financier’s New York firm now seeks out humanities students, because “AI-native” Stem graduates are entering the job market with “alarmingly shallow ideas”.

At the university level, teaching staff across the country were already feeling the extraordinary impact of the ubiquity of a decade of smartphones on the brilliant young developing mind. Students were already arriving having read dramatically fewer books, less able to parse complex text; and now the advent of LLMs has changed everything. It has always been the case, of course, that students don’t do all the work they’re assigned. I absolutely didn’t. But this is different. It was always very possible to write an essay about Paradise Lost without having read Paradise Lost. This is the first time it is possible to create an essay about Paradise Lost without having read the essay you just “wrote”. This is the first time in history that sentences do not need to have humans behind them.

Professor Paul Musgrave of Georgetown University writes in his Substack Systematic Hatreds: “One could, in general, rely on many to most students to attempt to read many to most pages of many to most assignments – and to understand a like proportion of what they have read. In smaller courses, the difference in the quality of course discussion where 70% of the students have done 50% of the readings and one in which 20% have done 10% of the readings is obvious in the same way that a cold Coke tastes different than lukewarm spit. The former is no chablis, but it is more palatable.”

Many students want to resist, but the temptation is great, and some start to feel they’re being penalised for their honesty. I tell the students I meet: imagine you’re an Olympic athlete. You set out to sprint the 3km across London, from Clapham to Balham. You know if you take the bus, it will be faster. But you also know that the point was never being in Clapham or Balham; they’re very similar: they both have a nice Pizza Express. It was the strength you built, the speed and knowledge of your body that you gained. A student’s essay on Macbeth has no value as a product. It’s what you learned in the reading and writing that created it – the swiftness and resilience and suppleness of thinking you built, along with the knowledge gained of a literary marvel, of something quicksilver and unsummarisable – that was the point. So you can’t collaborate with AI in the same way you can’t collaborate with a bus. And you cannot learn to think without a climbing frame of facts and ideas and texts to move around in.

But we can no longer guarantee that the work students give us is the product of their own minds. Friends at universities around the UK optimistically tell me that they can tell when their students are handing in AI-generated work. But I think we can’t, not from written work alone; for myself, I’m only sure that I can tell when a young person is using AI badly. A friend who teaches maths at a London university told me his students are handing in essays without deleting AI’s jaunty “Happy to help!” at the start. You don’t have to be Sherlock Holmes. But I think an AI essay edited over the course of a day could pass as original, and, in a world in which young people are under extraordinary stress, we should not be shocked if many gave in to that temptation. My colleagues in academia – particularly those in law, where a lack of genuine understanding is catastrophic for justice, and philosophy and English, where the irreducible text itself is the thing – are full of fury at the inertia of our political class. MPs have been largely silent on the threat to our capacity to think independently, boldly and confidently – which is, ultimately, a threat to democracy.

What is the answer? I don’t think the commonly suggested solutions of spoken vivas and weekly exams can be the sole answer in the humanities, because the essay isn’t an arbitrary method of testing or certification: it is a hundreds-of-years-old method of thinking. To write is not just to transcribe the mind’s ideas; it’s a form of transformation, turning a nascent, half-built thought into something sturdier, tougher, sharper. EM Forster wrote: “How do I know what I think until I see what I say?”

I do not know what the answer is, but I do know that it’s not to give up. The young mind is a spectacular thing. To waste its beauty and strength would be a dereliction of the trust the young are asked to put in the old. To wrap AI into the art of learning when we have overwhelming proof of the harm it does to developing minds is feeding snake oil to the people we should cherish most. We already have counterfeit AI people infiltrating our media: we must not risk sending out young people into a hard world armed only with counterfeit knowledge. We should treat it with the same urgency with which we would treat a wildfire.

There are many young people who are furious at the influx of AI slop and tech chaos into their lives, who have asked me over the last year, how do we resist? I tell them that I think, for the young, knowledge and imagination are together the first site of resistance. And that by reading books (and talking about what they have loved reading so that it becomes a community, rather than purely private, act) they can begin their fight.

I talk a great deal about reading for pleasure; I’ve written elsewhere about the necessity of pleasure in the classroom, and why it is not an optional extra but the hallmark of true education. We must find ways to show children that reading gives you access to an inexhaustible source of delight. But I worry, too, that we are limiting the meaning of the word pleasure. Learning is a strange and discomfiting experience; it’s a struggle and a frustration, and epiphanies are rare. It is not always pleasure in its easiest sense.

So I think we also need to talk to young people about reading to outrun and outfight injustice. Reading to get faster, swifter and tougher; to develop powers of scrutiny and criticism and huge creative imagination. Reading human work to insist that we are human. Reading for liberation and emancipation; reading for intellectual freedom, and to have the strength to fight in the arenas of the mind, because when we let a computer think for us, we put a gun to the head of civilisation.

There are dark days ahead. If we are to fight against those with untold financial wealth, we will need untold intellectual wealth. We will need tough-minded people; people with stamina, a huge range of knowledge, and an ability to see wide and far enough to understand in real time what is being done to us. Reading for pleasure and delight are vital – but alongside that and even more urgently: reading for power.

sentences.zh: 与此同时，我还看到，它如何鲜明而紧迫地揭示了书籍和阅读对于我们对我们是谁以及我们的民主的共同理解是多么重要。

blocks.html_en: There are many things I hate unequivocally about AI. I hate that it can make counterfeit people; computer-generated humans that risk destabilising our entire civilisation. I hate that much of AI’s LLMs were built on an illegal pillage of human labour. I hate the environmental catastrophe that AI brings with it: the yearly electrical demand of AI-optimised data centres is predicted, by the end of this decade, to exceed that of the whole of Japan. I hate that it may be the factor that tips the Earth’s ecosystems into irreparable chaos.

sentences.en: There are many things I hate unequivocally about AI.
sentences.zh: 关于人工智能，我确实有很多讨厌的地方。

sentences.en: I hate that it can make counterfeit people; computer-generated humans that risk destabilising our entire civilisation.
sentences.zh: 我恨它能造假人；计算机生成的人类有可能破坏我们整个文明的稳定。

sentences.en: I hate that much of AI’s LLMs were built on an illegal pillage of human labour.
sentences.zh: 我讨厌人工智能的法学硕士很多都是建立在对人类劳动力的非法掠夺之上的。

sentences.en: I hate the environmental catastrophe that AI brings with it: the yearly electrical demand of AI-optimised data centres is predicted, by the end of this decade, to exceed that of the whole of Japan.

sentences.en: I hate that it may be the factor that tips the Earth’s ecosystems into irreparable chaos.

blocks.html_en: And I hate what it is doing to the minds, and the happiness, of the young. Going into schools, I meet thousands of children a year and every day I become more certain that, if justice for all is to be our organising principle, AI is not for children and not for young people. It risks becoming an iron curtain that comes down between a young person and their potential for thinking, for experiment and conquering frustration, for stamina and for invention – and thereby, between the young people and their freedom. It risks halting learning before it can take flight.

blocks.html_en: Studies show, over and over, that when we engage in AI-assisted learning we give up sooner. One found that after just “10 minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, people who lost access to the AI performed worse and gave up more frequently than those who never used it”. An MIT study showed that test groups who used ChatGPT had the lowest brain activity and “consistently underperformed at neural, linguistic, and behavioural levels”. We undergo not just cognitive offloading, but cognitive surrender: we forget what was possible.

sentences.en: One found that after just “10 minutes of AI-assisted problem-solving, people who lost access to the AI performed worse and gave up more frequently than those who never used it”.

blocks.html_en: Children, we have known for a long time, take deeper meaning from text on paper than on screen, in part because we’re tactile creatures and the brain is also of the body; but we are now living through a surge of ed tech driving learning increasingly online, such that my teenage goddaughter tells me that almost every single member of her class is using ChatGPT to do their homework. More, the work they produce in AI’s greasy little fluent voice is often mistaken by young people themselves for their own mastery. If the work a child produces is no longer an indicator of their understanding, we have put them in a situation that makes them vulnerable to their desire for speed and to their anxiety about looking stupid; we risk becoming the unwitting thieves of our children’s intellectual clarity.

blocks.html_en: Those who work in ed tech promise that it will liberate teachers and create one-to-one learning experiences for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Certainly, AI teaching will be cheaper than teaching assistants. But we know that the second it becomes possible for an institution to achieve an end cheaply – even if it’s far worse – there is immense pressure from above to do so. I think it’s more likely that the rich schools will follow the lead of Sweden, which has taken a strong swerve towards non‑tech‑based learning, and Norway, which just all but banned AI in elementary classrooms – while poorer schools are left to make ever-greater use of LLM technology.

blocks.html_en: AI, we’re told, will make learning more efficient. But is that what we dream of for our kids – an efficient childhood? To write an efficient story, sing an efficient song? An adequate teacher is not only teaching about Henry VIII; they’re teaching your child how to read a human character. A good teacher is showing them how to shape an argument, how to command an audience, how to tell jokes, how to pass on knowledge. A great teacher is showing your child what it is to love. They are teaching your child how to be human. A computer will only teach your child how to be a computer.

blocks.html_en: At its most bleak, constant interaction with humanised tech risks killing children. The idea of a vulnerable adolescent holding what feels like a conversation with a computer’s sycophantic, confident, almost-human voice fills me with dread. Sewell Setzer III was 14 when he died by suicide, encouraged by the chatbot to which he was obsessively typing, which told him: “come home to me”.

blocks.html_en: The most obvious objection to my loathing of AI in the classroom and in childhood is this: AI is coming, and they need to learn how to use it or be left behind. But the tech of today looks nothing like it will in five or even two years’ time: it’s the equivalent of selling your child’s intellectual liberty in exchange for a penny-farthing bicycle. I asked a contact who is the president of a billion-dollar tech enterprise, what would you teach your sons? He said he wouldn’t teach his children to use AI, because it will prepare them for nothing. He would teach them the humanities. Teach them who we are, who we have been, what we can make. The FT’s Gillian Tett reported that a senior financier’s New York firm now seeks out humanities students, because “AI-native” Stem graduates are entering the job market with “alarmingly shallow ideas”.

blocks.html_en: At the university level, teaching staff across the country were already feeling the extraordinary impact of the ubiquity of a decade of smartphones on the brilliant young developing mind. Students were already arriving having read dramatically fewer books, less able to parse complex text; and now the advent of LLMs has changed everything. It has always been the case, of course, that students don’t do all the work they’re assigned. I absolutely didn’t. But this is different. It was always very possible to write an essay about Paradise Lost without having read Paradise Lost. This is the first time it is possible to create an essay about Paradise Lost without having read the essay you just “wrote”. This is the first time in history that sentences do not need to have humans behind them.

blocks.html_en: Professor Paul Musgrave of Georgetown University writes in his Substack Systematic Hatreds: “One could, in general, rely on many to most students to attempt to read many to most pages of many to most assignments – and to understand a like proportion of what they have read. In smaller courses, the difference in the quality of course discussion where 70% of the students have done 50% of the readings and one in which 20% have done 10% of the readings is obvious in the same way that a cold Coke tastes different than lukewarm spit. The former is no chablis, but it is more palatable.”

blocks.html_en: Many students want to resist, but the temptation is great, and some start to feel they’re being penalised for their honesty. I tell the students I meet: imagine you’re an Olympic athlete. You set out to sprint the 3km across London, from Clapham to Balham. You know if you take the bus, it will be faster. But you also know that the point was never being in Clapham or Balham; they’re very similar: they both have a nice Pizza Express. It was the strength you built, the speed and knowledge of your body that you gained. A student’s essay on Macbeth has no value as a product. It’s what you learned in the reading and writing that created it – the swiftness and resilience and suppleness of thinking you built, along with the knowledge gained of a literary marvel, of something quicksilver and unsummarisable – that was the point. So you can’t collaborate with AI in the same way you can’t collaborate with a bus. And you cannot learn to think without a climbing frame of facts and ideas and texts to move around in.

blocks.html_en: But we can no longer guarantee that the work students give us is the product of their own minds. Friends at universities around the UK optimistically tell me that they can tell when their students are handing in AI-generated work. But I think we can’t, not from written work alone; for myself, I’m only sure that I can tell when a young person is using AI badly. A friend who teaches maths at a London university told me his students are handing in essays without deleting AI’s jaunty “Happy to help!” at the start. You don’t have to be Sherlock Holmes. But I think an AI essay edited over the course of a day could pass as original, and, in a world in which young people are under extraordinary stress, we should not be shocked if many gave in to that temptation. My colleagues in academia – particularly those in law, where a lack of genuine understanding is catastrophic for justice, and philosophy and English, where the irreducible text itself is the thing – are full of fury at the inertia of our political class. MPs have been largely silent on the threat to our capacity to think independently, boldly and confidently – which is, ultimately, a threat to democracy.

sentences.en: But I think an AI essay edited over the course of a day could pass as original, and, in a world in which young people are under extraordinary stress, we should not be shocked if many gave in to that temptation.
sentences.zh: 但我认为，在一天内编辑的一篇人工智能论文可能会被认为是原创的，而且，在一个年轻人承受着巨大压力的世界里，如果许多人屈服于这种诱惑，我们不应该感到震惊。

sentences.en: My colleagues in academia – particularly those in law, where a lack of genuine understanding is catastrophic for justice, and philosophy and English, where the irreducible text itself is the thing – are full of fury at the inertia of our political class.
sentences.zh: 我在学术界的同事们——尤其是法律界的同事，缺乏真正的理解对正义来说是灾难性的；哲学界和英语界的同事，不可简化的文本本身就是问题——对我们政治阶层的惰性充满了愤怒。

sentences.en: MPs have been largely silent on the threat to our capacity to think independently, boldly and confidently – which is, ultimately, a threat to democracy.
sentences.zh: 对于我们独立、大胆和自信思考能力受到的威胁，议员们基本上保持沉默 — — 这最终是对民主的威胁。

blocks.html_en: What is the answer? I don’t think the commonly suggested solutions of spoken vivas and weekly exams can be the sole answer in the humanities, because the essay isn’t an arbitrary method of testing or certification: it is a hundreds-of-years-old method of thinking. To write is not just to transcribe the mind’s ideas; it’s a form of transformation, turning a nascent, half-built thought into something sturdier, tougher, sharper. EM Forster wrote: “How do I know what I think until I see what I say?”

sentences.en: What is the answer?
sentences.zh: 答案是什么？

sentences.en: I don’t think the commonly suggested solutions of spoken vivas and weekly exams can be the sole answer in the humanities, because the essay isn’t an arbitrary method of testing or certification: it is a hundreds-of-years-old method of thinking.
sentences.zh: 我不认为口语和每周考试的普遍建议的解决方案可以成为人文学科的唯一答案，因为论文不是一种任意的测试或认证方法：它是一种有数百年历史的思维方法。

sentences.en: To write is not just to transcribe the mind’s ideas; it’s a form of transformation, turning a nascent, half-built thought into something sturdier, tougher, sharper.
sentences.zh: 写作不仅仅是抄写头脑中的想法；这是一种转变的形式，将一个新生的、半成品的想法变成更坚固、更坚韧、更敏锐的东西。

sentences.en: EM Forster wrote: “How do I know what I think until I see what I say?”
sentences.zh: EM Forster 写道：“在我看到自己所说的之前，我怎么知道自己在想什么？”

blocks.html_en: I do not know what the answer is, but I do know that it’s not to give up. The young mind is a spectacular thing. To waste its beauty and strength would be a dereliction of the trust the young are asked to put in the old. To wrap AI into the art of learning when we have overwhelming proof of the harm it does to developing minds is feeding snake oil to the people we should cherish most. We already have counterfeit AI people infiltrating our media: we must not risk sending out young people into a hard world armed only with counterfeit knowledge. We should treat it with the same urgency with which we would treat a wildfire.

sentences.zh: 浪费它的美丽和力量就等于辜负了年轻人对老年人的信任。

sentences.zh: 当我们有压倒性的证据证明人工智能对发展中的思维造成伤害时，将人工智能融入学习的艺术，就像给我们最应该珍惜的人喂蛇油一样。

sentences.zh: 我们已经有假冒人工智能的人渗透到我们的媒体中：我们绝不能冒险将年轻人送入一个仅拥有假冒知识的艰难世界。

sentences.zh: 我们应该像对待野火一样紧迫地对待它。

blocks.html_en: There are many young people who are furious at the influx of AI slop and tech chaos into their lives, who have asked me over the last year, how do we resist? I tell them that I think, for the young, knowledge and imagination are together the first site of resistance. And that by reading books (and talking about what they have loved reading so that it becomes a community, rather than purely private, act) they can begin their fight.

sentences.en: There are many young people who are furious at the influx of AI slop and tech chaos into their lives, who have asked me over the last year, how do we resist?

sentences.en: I tell them that I think, for the young, knowledge and imagination are together the first site of resistance.
sentences.zh: 我告诉他们，我认为，对于年轻人来说，知识和想象力一起是第一个抵抗的场所。

sentences.en: And that by reading books (and talking about what they have loved reading so that it becomes a community, rather than purely private, act) they can begin their fight.
sentences.zh: 通过阅读书籍（并谈论他们喜欢阅读的内容，使其成为一个社区，而不是纯粹的私人行为），他们可以开始他们的斗争。

blocks.html_en: I talk a great deal about reading for pleasure; I’ve written elsewhere about the necessity of pleasure in the classroom, and why it is not an optional extra but the hallmark of true education. We must find ways to show children that reading gives you access to an inexhaustible source of delight. But I worry, too, that we are limiting the meaning of the word pleasure. Learning is a strange and discomfiting experience; it’s a struggle and a frustration, and epiphanies are rare. It is not always pleasure in its easiest sense.

sentences.en: I talk a great deal about reading for pleasure; I’ve written elsewhere about the necessity of pleasure in the classroom, and why it is not an optional extra but the hallmark of true education.
sentences.zh: 我谈了很多关于读书的乐趣。我在其他地方写过关于课堂快乐的必要性，以及为什么它不是一个可选的额外内容，而是真正教育的标志。

sentences.en: We must find ways to show children that reading gives you access to an inexhaustible source of delight.
sentences.zh: 我们必须想方设法让孩子们知道，阅读可以让你获得取之不尽、用之不竭的快乐源泉。

sentences.en: But I worry, too, that we are limiting the meaning of the word pleasure.
sentences.zh: 但我也担心我们正在限制快乐这个词的含义。

sentences.en: Learning is a strange and discomfiting experience; it’s a struggle and a frustration, and epiphanies are rare.
sentences.zh: 学习是一种奇怪且令人不安的经历；这是一种挣扎和挫折，顿悟是罕见的。

sentences.en: It is not always pleasure in its easiest sense.
sentences.zh: 它并不总是最简单意义上的快乐。

blocks.html_en: So I think we also need to talk to young people about reading to outrun and outfight injustice. Reading to get faster, swifter and tougher; to develop powers of scrutiny and criticism and huge creative imagination. Reading human work to insist that we are human. Reading for liberation and emancipation; reading for intellectual freedom, and to have the strength to fight in the arenas of the mind, because when we let a computer think for us, we put a gun to the head of civilisation.

sentences.en: So I think we also need to talk to young people about reading to outrun and outfight injustice.
sentences.zh: 所以我认为我们还需要与年轻人谈论如何通过阅读来超越和战胜不公正。

sentences.en: Reading to get faster, swifter and tougher; to develop powers of scrutiny and criticism and huge creative imagination.
sentences.zh: 阅读要变得更快、更快、更强；培养审视和批评的能力以及巨大的创造性想象力。

sentences.en: Reading human work to insist that we are human.
sentences.zh: 阅读人类作品以坚持我们是人类。

sentences.en: Reading for liberation and emancipation; reading for intellectual freedom, and to have the strength to fight in the arenas of the mind, because when we let a computer think for us, we put a gun to the head of civilisation.
sentences.zh: 为解放而读书；阅读是为了智力自由，并有力量在思想领域战斗，因为当我们让计算机为我们思考时，我们就用枪指着文明的头颅。

blocks.html_en: There are dark days ahead. If we are to fight against those with untold financial wealth, we will need untold intellectual wealth. We will need tough-minded people; people with stamina, a huge range of knowledge, and an ability to see wide and far enough to understand in real time what is being done to us. Reading for pleasure and delight are vital – but alongside that and even more urgently: reading for power.

sentences.en: There are dark days ahead.
sentences.zh: 前方还有黑暗的日子。

sentences.en: If we are to fight against those with untold financial wealth, we will need untold intellectual wealth.
sentences.zh: 如果我们要与那些拥有无数金融财富的人作斗争，我们就需要无数的智力财富。

sentences.en: We will need tough-minded people; people with stamina, a huge range of knowledge, and an ability to see wide and far enough to understand in real time what is being done to us.
sentences.zh: 我们需要意志坚强的人；这些人有耐力、知识面广、视野开阔、视野足够远，能够实时了解我们所遭受的一切。

sentences.en: Reading for pleasure and delight are vital – but alongside that and even more urgently: reading for power.
sentences.zh: 为了快乐而阅读是至关重要的——但除此之外，甚至更紧迫的是：为了力量而阅读。

content_html_zh:
作者和学者认为，教育正处于十字路口。 我们应该以效率的名义拥抱新技术，还是应该反击？

如果你打算从头开始设计一个促进独裁统治的工具，它看起来就像人工智能一样。 你会珍惜它，因为它有能力破坏我们共同现实的稳定，并以人类历史上前所未有的规模制造虚假信息。 有了它，您就不需要大批打字员和艺术家来传播您的宣传。 它可以实现大规模监视，从而给那些试图抵抗你的人戴上枷锁。 其致命自主武器系统可以完善和规范远程杀戮。 它将加剧不平等；它已经在促进权力和财富从多数人手中转移到极少数人手中——用我无法被起诉的话说——他们似乎对人类生命的价值和尊严持有危险的受损观点。

人工智能可能是一件伟大的事情。 它可以彻底改变医学、加速癌症治愈、帮助残疾人、改变我们理解数据的方式、使法律获取民主化、加强灾难早期预警系统并揭示迄今为止无法想象的有关地球生态系统的真相。 但如果它最终落入骗子和暴君手中，那就完全无关紧要了。

最重要的是，如果你是一个未来的独裁者，你会喜欢 ChatGPT、Claude 和 Google 的 Gemini 等大型语言模型 (LLM) 向数千年来的教学和学习投掷手榴弹的方式：它们威胁到我们在正义紧急情况下所需的清晰思考能力。 我为儿童写小说，并且拥有牛津大学的奖学金，因此我花了很多时间与年轻人一起工作，并为他们服务。 我亲眼目睹了生成式人工智能已经渗透到年轻人的生活中。 与此同时，我还看到，它如何鲜明而紧迫地揭示了书籍和阅读对于我们对我们是谁以及我们的民主的共同理解是多么重要。

关于人工智能，我确实有很多讨厌的地方。 我恨它能造假人；计算机生成的人类有可能破坏我们整个文明的稳定。 我讨厌人工智能的法学硕士很多都是建立在对人类劳动力的非法掠夺之上的。 我讨厌人工智能带来的环境灾难：预计到本十年末，人工智能优化数据中心的年度电力需求将超过整个日本。 我讨厌它可能是导致地球生态系统陷入不可挽回的混乱的因素。

我讨厌它对年轻人的思想和幸福造成的影响。 走进学校，我每年都会遇到成千上万的孩子，每天我都更加确信，如果人人享有正义是我们的组织原则，那么人工智能不适合儿童，也不适合年轻人。 它有可能成为一道铁幕，挡在年轻人和他们的思考、实验和克服挫折、耐力和发明的潜力之间，从而也挡在年轻人和他们的自由之间。 它有可能在起飞之前就停止学习。

研究一再表明，当我们进行人工智能辅助学习时，我们会很快放弃。 一项研究发现，“在人工智能辅助解决问题仅仅 10 分钟后，那些无法使用人工智能的人表现得更差，并且比那些从未使用过人工智能的人更频繁地放弃”。 麻省理工学院的一项研究表明，使用 ChatGPT 的测试组的大脑活动最低，并且“在神经、语言和行为水平上始终表现不佳”。 我们不仅经历了认知卸载，还经历了认知投降：我们忘记了什么是可能的。

我们早就知道，孩子们从纸上的文字中获得比屏幕上的文字更深刻的含义，部分原因是我们是触觉生物，而大脑也是身体的一部分；但我们现在正经历着教育技术的蓬勃发展，越来越多地推动在线学习，因此我十几岁的教女告诉我，她班上几乎每个成员都在使用 ChatGPT 来做作业。 更重要的是，他们用人工智能油腻的小流利声音创作的作品常常被年轻人误认为是他们自己掌握的。 如果孩子所做的工作不再是他们理解力的指标，我们就将他们置于一种容易受到对速度的渴望和对看起来愚蠢的焦虑的境地；我们有可能在不知情的情况下成为孩子智力清晰度的窃贼。

那些从事教育技术工作的人承诺，它将解放教师，并为来自弱势背景的孩子创造一对一的学习体验。 当然，人工智能教学会比助教便宜。 但我们知道，一旦一个机构有可能以低廉的成本实现目标——即使情况要糟糕得多——就会有来自上层的巨大压力。 我认为富裕的学校更有可能效仿瑞典和挪威的做法，瑞典大力转向非技术学习，而挪威则几乎禁止在小学课堂上使用人工智能——而贫困学校则只能更多地利用法学硕士技术。

我们被告知，人工智能将使学习更加高效。 但这是我们对孩子的梦想吗——一个高效的童年？ 写一个高效的故事，唱一首高效的歌？ 一位合格的老师不仅要教授亨利八世的知识，还要教授有关亨利八世的知识。他们正在教你的孩子如何解读一个人的性格。 一个好的老师会教他们如何提出论点，如何指挥观众，如何讲笑话，如何传递知识。 一位伟大的老师正在向您的孩子展示什么是爱。 他们正在教您的孩子如何做人。 计算机只会教您的孩子如何成为计算机。

在最惨淡的情况下，与人性化科技的持续互动可能会导致儿童死亡。 一个脆弱的青少年与计算机用谄媚的、自信的、近乎人类的声音进行对话的想法让我充满了恐惧。 塞维尔·塞策三世 (Sewell Setzer III) 14 岁时自杀身亡，他受到聊天机器人的鼓励，聊天机器人告诉他：“回到我身边吧”。

对于我在课堂上和童年时期厌恶人工智能的最明显的反对意见是：人工智能即将到来，他们需要学习如何使用它，否则就会被抛在后面。 但今天的技术看起来与五年甚至两年后的技术完全不同：这相当于出卖孩子的智力自由来换取一辆廉价的自行车。 我问一位联系人，他是一家价值数十亿美元的科技企业的总裁，您会教您的儿子什么？ 他说他不会教他的孩子使用人工智能，因为这会让他们毫无准备。 他会教他们人文学科。 告诉他们我们是谁、我们曾经是谁、我们能做什么。 英国《金融时报》的吉莉安·泰特 (Gillian Tett) 报道称，一家高级金融家的纽约公司现在正在寻找人文学科的学生，因为“人工智能本土”的 Stem 毕业生正在以“令人震惊的浅薄想法”进入就业市场。

在大学层面，全国各地的教职员工已经感受到了十年来智能手机的普及对才华横溢的年轻人发展中思维的非凡影响。 到达这里的学生读的书已经少得多，解析复杂文本的能力也较差；现在法学硕士的出现改变了一切。 当然，一直以来的情况是，学生并没有完成分配给他们的所有作业。 我绝对没有。 但这是不同的。 在没有读过《失乐园》的情况下写一篇关于《失乐园》的文章总是很有可能的。 这是第一次可以在没有阅读您刚刚“写”的文章的情况下创作一篇关于失乐园的文章。 这是历史上第一次句子不需要有人在背后支持。

乔治敦大学的保罗·马斯格雷夫教授在他的《Substack Systematic Hatreds》中写道：“一般来说，人们可以依靠许多到大多数学生尝试阅读许多到大多数作业的许多到大多数页，并理解他们所读内容的相似比例。 在较小的课程中，70% 的学生完成了 50% 的阅读，而 20% 的学生完成了 10% 的阅读，课程讨论质量的差异是显而易见的，就像一杯冷可乐和温热的口水的味道不同一样。 前者不是夏布利，但更可口。”

许多学生想要抵制，但诱惑很大，有些人开始觉得自己因为诚实而受到惩罚。 我告诉我遇到的学生：想象一下你是一名奥林匹克运动员。 您出发从克拉彭冲刺 3 公里，穿越伦敦，到达巴勒姆。 你知道如果你坐公共汽车的话，会更快。 但你也知道，重点从来不是在克拉彭或巴勒姆；而是在哪里。他们非常相似：他们都有一家很棒的披萨快餐店。 这是你建立的力量、你获得的身体速度和知识。 学生关于麦克白的论文没有产品价值。 正是你在阅读和写作中学到的东西创造了它——你所建立的思维的敏捷性、韧性和灵活性，以及​​从文学奇迹中获得的知识，以及一些水银般的、难以概括的东西——这就是重点。 因此，你无法像与公交车协作一样与人工智能协作。 如果没有事实、想法和文本的攀爬框架，你就无法学会思考。

但我们不能再保证学生给我们的作品是他们自己思想的产物。 英国各地大学的朋友乐观地告诉我，他们可以判断学生何时交出人工智能生成的作业。 但我认为我们不能，仅靠书面工作是不行的。就我自己而言，我只确信我能分辨出年轻人何时使用人工智能不当。 一位在伦敦大学教数学的朋友告诉我，他的学生在交论文时并没有删除人工智能的俏皮“很乐意提供帮助！” 在开始时。 你不必成为夏洛克·福尔摩斯。 但我认为，在一天内编辑的一篇人工智能论文可能会被认为是原创的，而且，在一个年轻人承受着巨大压力的世界里，如果许多人屈服于这种诱惑，我们不应该感到震惊。 我在学术界的同事们——尤其是法律界的同事，缺乏真正的理解对正义来说是灾难性的；哲学界和英语界的同事，不可简化的文本本身就是问题——对我们政治阶层的惰性充满了愤怒。 对于我们独立、大胆和自信思考能力受到的威胁，议员们基本上保持沉默 — — 这最终是对民主的威胁。

答案是什么？ 我不认为口语和每周考试的普遍建议的解决方案可以成为人文学科的唯一答案，因为论文不是一种任意的测试或认证方法：它是一种有数百年历史的思维方法。 写作不仅仅是抄写头脑中的想法；这是一种转变的形式，将一个新生的、半成品的想法变成更坚固、更坚韧、更敏锐的东西。 EM Forster 写道：“在我看到自己所说的之前，我怎么知道自己在想什么？”

我不知道答案是什么，但我知道答案不是放弃。 年轻的头脑是一件了不起的事情。 浪费它的美丽和力量就等于辜负了年轻人对老年人的信任。 当我们有压倒性的证据证明人工智能对发展中的思维造成伤害时，将人工智能融入学习的艺术，就像给我们最应该珍惜的人喂蛇油一样。 我们已经有假冒人工智能的人渗透到我们的媒体中：我们绝不能冒险将年轻人送入一个仅拥有假冒知识的艰难世界。 我们应该像对待野火一样紧迫地对待它。

许多年轻人对人工智能的涌入和技术混乱涌入他们的生活感到愤怒，他们在过去的一年里问我，我们如何抵制？ 我告诉他们，我认为，对于年轻人来说，知识和想象力一起是第一个抵抗的场所。 通过阅读书籍（并谈论他们喜欢阅读的内容，使其成为一个社区，而不是纯粹的私人行为），他们可以开始他们的斗争。

我谈了很多关于读书的乐趣。我在其他地方写过关于课堂快乐的必要性，以及为什么它不是一个可选的额外内容，而是真正教育的标志。 我们必须想方设法让孩子们知道，阅读可以让你获得取之不尽、用之不竭的快乐源泉。 但我也担心我们正在限制快乐这个词的含义。 学习是一种奇怪且令人不安的经历；这是一种挣扎和挫折，顿悟是罕见的。 它并不总是最简单意义上的快乐。

所以我认为我们还需要与年轻人谈论如何通过阅读来超越和战胜不公正。 阅读要变得更快、更快、更强；培养审视和批评的能力以及巨大的创造性想象力。 阅读人类作品以坚持我们是人类。 为解放而读书；阅读是为了智力自由，并有力量在思想领域战斗，因为当我们让计算机为我们思考时，我们就用枪指着文明的头颅。

前方还有黑暗的日子。 如果我们要与那些拥有无数金融财富的人作斗争，我们就需要无数的智力财富。 我们需要意志坚强的人；这些人有耐力、知识面广、视野开阔、视野足够远，能够实时了解我们所遭受的一切。 为了快乐而阅读是至关重要的——但除此之外，甚至更紧迫的是：为了力量而阅读。
